notes.definition: Many transition metals have ions with different charges, form coloured compounds and are useful as catalysts. These typical properties can be shown using compounds of chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel and copper.
explanation: Transition metals share three typical properties that make them different from Group 1 and Group 2 metals. First, many transition metals can form ions with different charges. Second, their compounds are usually coloured. Third, the metals and their compounds are often useful as catalysts. You need to be able to give examples of each property using compounds of chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel and copper.

A Group 1 metal always forms a 1+ ion and a Group 2 metal always forms a 2+ ion. Many transition metals, however, can form more than one ion. Iron forms Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions, and copper forms Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺ ions. The charge is shown in the name using a Roman numeral. Iron(II) oxide is FeO and iron(III) oxide is Fe₂O₃; iron(II) chloride is FeCl₂ and iron(III) chloride is FeCl₃. Copper(I) oxide is Cu₂O and copper(II) oxide is CuO. Chromium commonly forms Cr³⁺, and cobalt and nickel commonly form Co²⁺ and Ni²⁺.

To work out a formula, balance the charges. In iron(III) oxide, each Fe³⁺ ion has a charge of 3+ and each oxide ion O²⁻ has a charge of 2−. Two Fe³⁺ ions (total 6+) balance three O²⁻ ions (total 6−), giving Fe₂O₃. Working backwards, you can find the charge on a transition metal ion from a formula: in CuCl₂ there are two Cl⁻ ions (2−), so copper must be Cu²⁺.

Compounds of transition metals are often coloured, while compounds of Group 1 and Group 2 metals are usually white and dissolve to give colourless solutions. Copper(II) sulfate is blue, iron(II) compounds are pale green, iron(III) compounds are orange-brown (the colour of rust), nickel(II) compounds are green, cobalt(II) chloride solution is pink and potassium manganate(VII) is purple. Different ions of the same metal can have different colours, as with Fe²⁺ (green) and Fe³⁺ (orange-brown). Coloured transition metal compounds are used in pigments, paints, pottery glazes and stained glass, and give colour to gemstones such as rubies (chromium) and emeralds.

A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up in the reaction. Many transition metals and their compounds are good catalysts. Iron is the catalyst in the Haber process for making ammonia: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). Nickel is the catalyst used to harden vegetable oils by reacting them with hydrogen to make margarine. Manganese(IV) oxide, MnO₂, catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). At the end of the reaction the catalyst has the same mass and is chemically unchanged.

Catalysts are very important in industry because they allow reactions to happen quickly at lower temperatures. This saves energy and money, and reduces the use of fossil fuels. Because a catalyst is not used up, only a small amount is needed and it can be used again and again. This is a major reason why transition metals are so economically important.
keyFacts: Many transition metals form ions with different charges, for example Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺.
Roman numerals show the charge: iron(III) chloride contains Fe³⁺ and is FeCl₃.
Iron(II) oxide is FeO; iron(III) oxide is Fe₂O₃; copper(I) oxide is Cu₂O; copper(II) oxide is CuO.
Transition metal compounds are usually coloured; Group 1 compounds are usually white.
Copper(II) sulfate is blue, iron(II) compounds pale green, iron(III) compounds orange-brown.
Transition metals and their compounds are useful catalysts.
Iron: Haber process catalyst. Nickel: hydrogenation of vegetable oils. MnO₂: decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.
A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up, so its mass is unchanged at the end.
Catalysts allow lower temperatures, saving energy and cost.

keyTerms.definition: A metal from the central block of the periodic table, such as Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni or Cu.
A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up.
A charged particle formed when an atom loses or gains electrons.
Shows the charge on a metal ion in a compound, for example (II) in iron(II) sulfate means Fe²⁺.
A coloured substance used to give colour to paints, inks, glass or glazes; many contain transition metal compounds.
The industrial process that makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen using an iron catalyst.
Adding hydrogen to a substance, for example to harden vegetable oils into margarine using a nickel catalyst.

workedExamples.title: Writing a formula from a name
workedExamples.question: Write the formula of iron(III) oxide.
steps: Iron(III) means the iron ion is Fe³⁺. Oxide is O²⁻.
Find the lowest common multiple of 3 and 2: 6.
Two Fe³⁺ ions give 6+; three O²⁻ ions give 6−.
The charges cancel, so the formula is Fe₂O₃.

workedExamples.title: Finding the charge on a metal ion
workedExamples.question: Copper forms an oxide with the formula Cu₂O. Work out the charge on the copper ion and name the compound.
steps: Oxide ion is O²⁻, so the total negative charge is 2−.
Two copper ions must give a total of 2+.
So each copper ion is Cu⁺.

workedExamples.title: Relative formula mass and percentage of metal
workedExamples.question: Calculate the relative formula mass of Fe₂O₃ and the percentage by mass of iron in it. (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16)
steps: Percentage of iron = (mass of iron in formula ÷ Mr) × 100.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the Roman numeral in iron(III) oxide means there are three iron atoms.
misconceptions.right: In fact the Roman numeral gives the charge on the ion (Fe³⁺). Iron(III) oxide is Fe₂O₃, with two iron ions.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a catalyst is used up or changed in a reaction.
misconceptions.right: In fact a catalyst is chemically unchanged and has the same mass at the end, so it can be reused.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all compounds of metals are coloured.
misconceptions.right: In fact compounds of Group 1 and Group 2 metals are usually white or colourless; coloured compounds are typical of transition metals.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think each transition metal can only form one ion, like sodium.
misconceptions.right: In fact many transition metals form ions with different charges, such as Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, so the name must state which ion is present.

realWorld: Iron catalysts in the Haber process make ammonia for fertilisers that help feed a large part of the world's population.
Nickel catalysts are used to turn liquid vegetable oils into spreadable margarine.
Cobalt compounds give the deep blue colour to some glass and pottery; chromium compounds give rubies their red colour.
Copper compounds give the blue-green colour (verdigris) of old copper roofs and statues.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is for separate Chemistry (8462) only.
Typical properties: ions with different charges, coloured compounds, and use as catalysts, exemplified with compounds of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni and Cu.
examTips: Learn the three properties as a set: ions with different charges, coloured compounds, catalysts. Give a named example for each.
For catalysts, name the metal and the process: iron in the Haber process; nickel in hydrogenating oils; manganese(IV) oxide in decomposing hydrogen peroxide.
Use Roman numerals to work out charges, then balance charges to write formulae.
Do not describe a catalyst as 'taking part and being used up'; say it speeds up the reaction without being used up.
summary: Many transition metals form ions with different charges (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺, Cu⁺/Cu²⁺).
Roman numerals in names show the charge on the metal ion.
Transition metal compounds are usually coloured.
Transition metals and their compounds are useful catalysts.
Examples: iron (Haber process), nickel (margarine), manganese(IV) oxide (hydrogen peroxide).

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a typical property of transition metals?
options: They react vigorously with cold water
They form ions with different charges
markScheme: 1 mark: they react vigorously with cold water
questions.explanation: Vigorous reaction with water is typical of Group 1. The other three are the typical properties of transition metals.

questions.question: What colour is copper(II) sulfate solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: blue
questions.explanation: Copper(II) compounds are typically blue. Orange-brown is typical of iron(III) and purple of potassium manganate(VII).

questions.question: What is a catalyst?
options: A substance that slows down a reaction
A reactant that is used up quickly
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up
A product of a fast reaction
markScheme: 1 mark: speeds up a reaction without being used up
questions.explanation: A catalyst increases the rate and is unchanged at the end, so it is not a reactant or product.

questions.question: Which element forms coloured compounds?
markScheme: 1 mark: cobalt
questions.explanation: Cobalt is a transition metal. Compounds of sodium, magnesium and aluminium are white or colourless.

questions.question: Which transition metal is used as the catalyst in the Haber process for making ammonia?
markScheme: 1 mark: iron
questions.explanation: Iron catalyses N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Nickel is used for hydrogenating vegetable oils.

questions.question: What is the formula of iron(III) oxide?
markScheme: 1 mark: Fe₂O₃
questions.explanation: Iron(III) is Fe³⁺ and oxide is O²⁻. Two Fe³⁺ (6+) balance three O²⁻ (6−). FeO is iron(II) oxide.

questions.question: Nickel is used as a catalyst in which process?
options: Hydrogenating vegetable oils to make margarine
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrogenating vegetable oils
questions.explanation: Nickel catalyses the reaction of vegetable oils with hydrogen. Iron is used for ammonia and MnO₂ for hydrogen peroxide.

questions.question: A solution contains Fe³⁺ ions. What colour is it most likely to be?
markScheme: 1 mark: orange-brown
questions.explanation: Iron(III) compounds are orange-brown (like rust). Pale green is typical of iron(II), and blue of copper(II).

questions.question: Which pair shows ions of the same element with different charges?
markScheme: 1 mark: Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺
questions.explanation: Only iron appears twice with different charges. The other pairs are different elements from the same group.

questions.question: 0.5 g of manganese(IV) oxide is added to hydrogen peroxide. Oxygen is given off rapidly. What is the mass of manganese(IV) oxide at the end of the reaction?
options: 0 g, because it was used up
More than 0.5 g, because it gained oxygen
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.5 g
questions.explanation: MnO₂ is a catalyst. It is not used up, so its mass is unchanged and it can be recovered by filtering.

questions.question: What does the (II) in copper(II) oxide tell you?
options: The copper ion has a 2+ charge
markScheme: 1 mark: copper ion has a 2+ charge
questions.explanation: The Roman numeral gives the ion's charge. Copper(II) oxide is CuO, with one Cu²⁺ and one O²⁻.

questions.question: A student adds 0.80 g of manganese(IV) oxide catalyst to hydrogen peroxide solution. When the reaction stops, the manganese(IV) oxide is filtered off and dried. What mass of manganese(IV) oxide should be recovered?
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.80 g
questions.explanation: A catalyst is not used up, so the same mass is recovered (ignoring small losses during filtering).

questions.question: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of iron(III) chloride, FeCl₃. (Ar: Fe = 56, Cl = 35.5)
questions.explanation: 56 + 106.5 = 162.5. Remember to multiply chlorine by 3.

questions.question: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄. (Ar: Cu = 63.5, S = 32, O = 16)
Iron forms a chloride with the formula FeCl₃. What is the size of the charge on the iron ion in this compound? (Give the number only.)
markScheme: 1 mark: 3 (Fe³⁺)
questions.explanation: Three Cl⁻ ions give 3−, so iron must be 3+. The compound is iron(III) chloride.

questions.question: Copper forms an oxide with the formula Cu₂O. Work out the size of the charge on each copper ion. (Give the number only.)
markScheme: 1 mark: oxide ion is O²⁻ so total positive charge is 2+
1 mark: shared between 2 copper ions, so 1 (Cu⁺)
questions.explanation: Two copper ions balance one O²⁻, so each must be 1+. The compound is copper(I) oxide.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage by mass of iron in iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃. (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16)
markScheme: 1 mark: mass of iron = 112
questions.explanation: Use the total mass of iron in the formula (two atoms, 112), not just one atom.

questions.question: Give the three typical properties of transition metals and their compounds.
markScheme: 1 mark: form ions with different charges
1 mark: form coloured compounds
1 mark: useful as catalysts
questions.explanation: These are the three properties named in the specification.

questions.question: Name the transition metal compound used as a catalyst to decompose hydrogen peroxide.
markScheme: 1 mark: manganese(IV) oxide / MnO₂
questions.explanation: MnO₂ speeds up 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ and is not used up.

questions.question: Write the formulae of iron(II) chloride and iron(III) chloride.
markScheme: 1 mark: FeCl₂
1 mark: FeCl₃
questions.explanation: Iron(II) is Fe²⁺, needing two Cl⁻; iron(III) is Fe³⁺, needing three Cl⁻.

questions.question: Explain why catalysts are useful in industrial processes.
markScheme: 1 mark: they increase the rate of reaction / allow reactions at lower temperatures
1 mark: so they save energy and money / they are not used up so can be reused
questions.explanation: Faster reactions at lower temperatures mean more product for less energy.

questions.question: A student wants to show that copper(II) sulfate acts as a catalyst for the reaction between zinc and dilute sulfuric acid. Describe two observations or measurements that would show this.
markScheme: 1 mark: the reaction is faster (more bubbles of hydrogen per minute) with copper(II) sulfate than without it
1 mark: the copper compound is not used up / the same amount is present at the end
questions.explanation: A catalyst must speed up the reaction and remain unchanged.

questions.question: A technician has two unlabelled white powders, sodium sulfate and anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. When water is added, one forms a blue solution and the other forms a colourless solution. Identify which is which and explain your reasoning.
markScheme: 1 mark: the blue solution is copper(II) sulfate and the colourless solution is sodium sulfate
1 mark: copper is a transition metal, which forms coloured compounds; sodium (Group 1) compounds are colourless in solution
questions.explanation: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is white but turns blue with water, a typical coloured transition metal compound.

questions.question:
Iron rusts to form hydrated iron(III) oxide. Old rust is orange-brown, but some iron compounds formed in the early stages of corrosion are pale green.
Use your knowledge of iron ions to suggest an explanation for the two colours.
markScheme: 1 mark: iron forms ions with different charges, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺
1 mark: iron(II) (Fe²⁺) compounds are pale green
1 mark: iron(III) (Fe³⁺) compounds are orange-brown, so the colour changes as Fe²⁺ is converted to Fe³⁺
questions.explanation: This links two typical properties: ions with different charges and coloured compounds.

questions.question: Describe the typical properties of transition metals and their compounds. Use examples from chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel and copper in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: many form ions with different charges, for example Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺; shown by Roman numerals, for example iron(II) chloride FeCl₂ and iron(III) chloride FeCl₃, copper(I) oxide Cu₂O and copper(II) oxide CuO; form coloured compounds, for example copper(II) sulfate blue, iron(II) pale green, iron(III) orange-brown, nickel(II) green, cobalt(II) pink, potassium manganate(VII) purple, chromium(III) green; useful as catalysts, for example iron in the Haber process, nickel in hydrogenating vegetable oils, manganese(IV) oxide decomposing hydrogen peroxide; catalysts speed up reactions without being used up; contrast with Group 1 (single 1+ ion, white compounds).
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all three properties described clearly with several correct, specific examples.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): two or three properties described with at least one correct example.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two properties stated with few or no examples.
questions.explanation: Structure the answer in three parts, one per property, each with a named example.

questions.question:
Iron forms two oxides, FeO and Fe₂O₃, and two chlorides, FeCl₂ and FeCl₃. Sodium forms only one oxide, Na₂O, and one chloride, NaCl.
Explain these observations, naming the iron compounds and showing how the charges balance in each formula.
markScheme: Indicative content: iron is a transition metal and forms ions with different charges, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺; FeO is iron(II) oxide: one Fe²⁺ balances one O²⁻; Fe₂O₃ is iron(III) oxide: two Fe³⁺ (6+) balance three O²⁻ (6−); FeCl₂ is iron(II) chloride: Fe²⁺ balances two Cl⁻; FeCl₃ is iron(III) chloride: Fe³⁺ balances three Cl⁻; sodium is in Group 1 and only forms Na⁺ (loses its single outer electron), so only Na₂O (two Na⁺ balance O²⁻) and NaCl.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains different charges for iron with correct names and charge balancing for most formulae, and contrasts with sodium.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that iron forms different ions, with limited naming or charge balancing.
questions.explanation: The total positive and negative charges in each formula must be equal.

questions.question:
Transition metals and their compounds are used as catalysts in many industrial processes.
Evaluate the use of transition metal catalysts in industry. Include named examples in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: examples: iron in the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃) for fertilisers; nickel for hydrogenating vegetable oils to make margarine; manganese(IV) oxide for decomposing hydrogen peroxide; advantages: increase the rate of reaction, so more product in a given time; allow lower temperatures, saving energy and fuel, reducing costs and carbon dioxide emissions; not used up, so small amounts can be reused many times; disadvantages: some transition metals are expensive or toxic (for example nickel, cobalt, chromium compounds); catalyst may need to be separated from the product (for example nickel from margarine); catalysts eventually need replacing or cleaning; mining the metals has environmental costs; judgement: benefits usually outweigh costs, which is why catalysts are used so widely.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): balanced evaluation with several advantages and disadvantages, named examples, and a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some advantages and at least one disadvantage, with at least one example.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'catalysts speed up reactions', with no evaluation.
questions.explanation: Evaluate questions need both sides and a conclusion. Link each advantage to cost, energy or the environment.
